title: cumulative impact of cover crops on soil carbon sequestration and profitability in a temperate humid climate

question.value: The objectives of this study were to (i) evaluate the cumulative effects of CC on soil C sequestration, primary productivity, and profit margins, and (ii) determine if current and projected C prices may be an effective strategy for incentivising the quantity of soil C sequestered by CCs.
question.quote: The objectives of this study were to (i) evaluate the cumulative effects of CC on soil C sequestration, primary productivity, and profit margins, and (ii) determine if current and projected C prices may be an effective strategy for incentivising the quantity of soil C sequestered by CCs.

method.value: To meet these objectives, a long-term CC experiment located at Ridgetown, Ontario Canada, established in 2007 and repeated at an adjacent site in 2008 was utilized.
method.quote: To meet these objectives, a long-term CC experiment located at Ridgetown, Ontario Canada, established in 2007 and repeated at an adjacent site in 2008 was utilized.

sample.value: The experiment at both sites consisted of 20 main plots (5 CC treatment × 4 replications) and 40 split-plots (5 CC treatment × 4 replications × 2 crop residue or N fertilizer treatment).
sample.quote: The experiment at both sites consisted of 20 main plots (5 CC treatment × 4 replications) and 40 split-plots (5 CC treatment × 4 replications × 2 crop residue or N fertilizer treatment).

finding.value: Total amount of plant C added to soil with CCs translated into greater soil organic carbon (SOC) content by 10–20 Mg C ha−1 than the no-CC control across both sites.

title: Cover crops improve soil structure and change organic carbon distribution in macroaggregate fractions

question.value: Investigate the legacy effect of cover crops on soil aggregates after three crop rotations in the second main crop (winter wheat) after the last cover crop treatment.
question.quote: This study entailed an investigation of the legacy effect of CCs on soil aggregates after three crop rotations in the second main crop (winter wheat) after the last CC treatment.

method.value: The experiment used a fully randomized block design with three field replications per treatment, measuring aggregate stability via dry and wet sieving and organic carbon distribution in macroaggregate fractions.
method.quote: The experiment was conducted as a fully randomized block design with three field replications per treatment.

sample.value: 21 plots (9 m × 9 m) with seven cover crop treatments (fallow, mustard, phacelia, oat, clover, Mix4, Mix12) sampled at three soil depths (0–10, 10–20, 30–40 cm) with three replicates each.
sample.quote: In total, 21 plots, 9 m× 9 m in size (including 0.7 m edges), were sampled for this study.

finding.value: All cover crops increased mean weight diameter (MWD) by 10–19% compared to fallow, with mixtures (16%) showing a slightly higher average increase than single species (12%).
finding.quote: The results showed that, compared to the fallow, all CCs increased the MWD between 10 % and 19 % in soil under the following main crop.

title: cover crops and chicken grazing in a winter fallow field improve soil carbon and nitrogen contents and decrease methane emissions

question.value: The study aims to improve soil carbon and nitrogen availability, increase rice grain yield, and reduce CH4 emissions in the rice growing season using cover crops with chicken grazing in a winter fallow field.
question.quote: In this study, using a symbiotic farming practice with cover crops with chicken grazing in a winter fallow field, we aim to (i) improve soil carbon and nitrogen availability, (ii) increase rice grain yield, and (iii) reduce CH4 emissions in the rice growing season.

method.value: A randomized block experiment with three treatments: cover crops with chicken grazing (+C), cover crops without chicken grazing (−C), and bare fallow field (CK).
method.quote: A randomized block experiment was established with 3 different treatments, including cover crops (Lolium spp. and Astragalus sinicus) with chicken grazing (+ C), cover crops without chicken grazing (− C), and a bare, fallow field (CK).

sample.value: Each field plot was 140 m2 with three replications.
sample.quote: Each field plot covers 140 m2, and there were three replications.

finding.value: The +C treatment increased rice yield by 3.8% over −C and 12.3% over CK, and reduced CH4 emissions by 26.9% over −C and 10.6% over CK.
finding.quote: The annual rice grain yield of the + C treatment was 3.8% higher than that of the − C treatment and 12.3% higher than that of the bare fallow field (CK), while the annual CH4 emissions of the + C treatment were 26.9% lower than those of the − C treatment and 10.6% lower than those of the CK treatment.
